What is different about this edition?

Your four notebooks
1) Concept Notebook - definitions, formulas and mechanisms. 2) Chart Notebook - annotations/replay. 3) Macro
Notebook - central banks, data and weekly views. 4) Trading Journal - only when the course reaches
simulated/live execution.
What "source of truth" means
Use the course as the source of truth for the learning and testing process. Time-sensitive facts - broker
licenses, product terms, platform features, tax rules, regulations and central-bank frameworks - must be
rechecked against the official links preserved in the course before you act on them.
Important navigation note
The original course pages retain their printed page numbers. This guided edition adds pages around them,
so use the PDF bookmarks for fast navigation. The original Table of Contents and all original appendices,
formulas, worksheets, quiz answers, gate frameworks and bibliography are retained.
No skipping rule
If you cannot explain a topic in your own words, calculate it where required, or pass the relevant gate, the correct
action is to repeat the material - not to move to a more exciting chapter.

Chapter 1
How to Use This Course
This course is designed to be followed sequentially, not sampled like a collection of trading tips. It
expands the supplied 49-page reference framework, A Practical Forex Trading Roadmap for a Kenyan
Retail Trader, into a complete learning program. The original framework’s strongest ideas are retained:
learn mechanics before setups; treat trading rules as testable hypotheses; use conservative risk; require
historical evidence; complete at least 100 serious demo trades; measure rule adherence; and move to tiny
live exposure only after objective gates are passed.
The course deliberately postpones programming, Expert Advisors, Python, machine learning and auto-
mated optimization. Those tools are useful only after you understand the market, risk, strategy design
and evidence well enough to know what you are asking a computer to test. The final chapter defines the
knowledge gate required before beginning that separate IT/systematic track.
1.1 What this document is - and is not
This is a learning framework and reference manual , not a promise of profit, a signal service, or
personalized investment advice. Retail leveraged FX/CFD trading has a high loss rate. Kenya’s Capital
Markets Authority regulates online foreign-exchange intermediaries, and the U.S. CFTC reports that
roughly two out of three retail OTC forex customers lose money after costs. Those facts are not reasons
to stop learning; they are reasons to learn with unusually strict standards.
Treat this document as your source of truth for the process of learning and testing , but not for facts
that can change after publication. Broker licenses, product terms, tax law, platform features, central-bank
policy frameworks and regulations must be rechecked against the live oﬀicial links in the Resource Library
before you act on them.
1.2 The rule for progression
Time does not grant permission to advance. Evidence does. If a phase is scheduled for four weeks
but you cannot pass its gate, repeat it. If a strategy fails testing, reject it. If your demo execution
is undisciplined, stay on demo. If your live results diverge materially from your validated assumptions,
reduce risk and investigate.
A useful mantra for the entire course is:

Chapter 1 - What Forex Actually Is
The rule for this session
Do not ask for a setup yet. First understand what the product is, how the quote works, how orders are executed,
and where cost and leverage enter.
What you must be able to do before moving on
By the end of this chapter you should be able to explain what an exchange rate represents, distinguish
currency exchange from speculative trading, identify the main forms of FX instruments, and explain why the
retail platform on your screen is only one small interface into a much larger market.
Notebook setup
Use your Concept Notebook. Write the chapter title and date. Leave a margin for corrections. Do not merely
copy definitions; after each major section, restate the idea in your own words.
Before you read
1
Without looking ahead, write what you currently think "What Forex Actually Is" means.
2
Write one reason this topic could affect trading decisions, risk, or interpretation.
3
Write one mistake a beginner might make if this topic is misunderstood.
Slow first-principles walkthrough
Start with the simplest possible idea: foreign exchange is the exchange of one currency for another. A
currency price is never meaningful by itself. EUR/USD = 1.1700 means one euro is priced at 1.1700 U.S.
dollars. If that pair rises, the euro has strengthened relative to the dollar (equivalently, the dollar has
weakened relative to the euro). The word relative is the anchor: a currency can be strong against one
currency and weak against another at the same time.
Next separate economic need from speculation. Importers, exporters, investors, banks and central banks
create real currency exposures. A hedge attempts to reduce an exposure that already exists; a speculator
deliberately accepts exposure in the hope of profiting from price movement. That distinction explains why
risk control becomes non-negotiable for a retail trader: unlike an importer who must obtain a currency, the
trader chose the risk.
Finally, do not confuse the retail platform with the market itself. The global FX market includes spot,
forwards, swaps, futures and options, and a retail OTC product can differ legally and operationally from
deliverable bank-to-bank spot FX. Your job in this chapter is not to memorize labels; it is to understand what
each instrument is for and what kind of market structure you are entering.

Chapter 2
Chapter 1 - What Forex Actually Is
2.1 Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you should be able to explain what an exchange rate represents, distinguish
currency exchange from speculative trading, identify the main forms of FX instruments, and explain why
the retail platform on your screen is only one small interface into a much larger market.
2.2 First principle: a currency is a price relative to another currency
A currency has no exchange value in isolation. The statement “the euro is 1.17” is incomplete. One euro
equals 1.17 what? In FX, value is expressed as a pair. If EUR/USD is 1.1700, one euro is worth 1.1700
U.S. dollars at that quoted moment.
This relative nature is the core of every FX trade. If EUR/USD rises, either the euro has strengthened
relative to the dollar, the dollar has weakened relative to the euro, or both forces are operating together.
A trader must resist simplistic statements such as “the euro is strong” without asking: strong against
which currency , over what horizon, and for what reason?
2.3 Why currencies need to be exchanged
Foreign exchange exists because households, firms, governments and investors conduct transactions across
currency areas. Examples include:
• a Kenyan importer paying a European supplier in euros;
• an American fund buying Japanese bonds and converting dollars into yen;
• a British tourist paying expenses in U.S. dollars;
• a multinational company hedging future revenue received in another currency;
• a central bank managing reserves;
• a trader taking a view on how two currencies may reprice.
Speculation is therefore only one use of the FX market. The underlying market exists because the world
economy constantly creates currency exposures.

Forex Trading From First Principles to Advanced Practice Version 1.0
2.4 How large is the market?
The Bank for International Settlements’ 2025 Triennial Survey reported average OTC FX turnover of
about USD 9.6 trillion per day in April 2025 . The U.S. dollar was on one side of roughly 89% of
transactions. Spot trading was only part of that total; FX swaps and forwards also represented enormous
activity.
This matters because “forex” is not synonymous with “retail traders on MetaTrader. ” The institutional
market includes banks, dealers, asset managers, hedge funds, corporations, central banks and many other
participants with different objectives and time horizons.
Oﬀicial source: BIS - OTC foreign exchange turnover in April 2025
2.5 The main FX instruments
2.5.1 Spot FX
A spot transaction is an agreement to exchange one currency for another at the prevailing spot rate, con-
ventionally settling shortly after the trade depending on the pair and market convention. Retail platforms
often use the language of “spot forex,” but the legal/economic product offered to a retail customer may
be an OTC leveraged contract or CFD rather than a deliverable bank-to-bank spot transaction. Always
read the broker’s product disclosure.
2.5.2 Outright forwards
A forward fixes an exchange rate today for an exchange of currencies at a future date. Corporations
use forwards to hedge known future currency flows. Forward pricing is closely related to interest-rate
differentials between the two currencies.
2.5.3 FX swaps
An FX swap combines one currency exchange with a reverse exchange at a later date. These are heavily
used for funding and liquidity management. BIS data show that FX swaps are a major share of global
FX turnover.
2.5.4 Currency futures
Futures are standardized exchange-traded contracts. Unlike decentralized OTC spot trading, futures
trade on regulated exchanges with central clearing, standardized contract specifications and transparent
exchange rules. CME provides extensive free education on FX futures even if you ultimately trade retail
spot/CFDs.
Oﬀicial learning source: CME - Introduction to FX
2.5.5 Currency options
An option gives the holder a right, but not an obligation, to transact under specified terms. Options
introduce concepts such as implied volatility, strike price, expiry, delta and skew. You do not need to
trade options to benefit from understanding what option markets can reveal about expected volatility and
hedging demand.
33

Forex Trading From First Principles to Advanced Practice Version 1.0
2.6 OTC versus exchange-traded
A crucial distinction is whether the product trades through a centralized exchange or over the counter
(OTC). Retail OTC forex customers generally transact through a dealer/broker arrangement rather than
sending an order to one universal global FX exchange. The CFTC specifically warns retail traders to
understand this structure and the role of the dealer.
Oﬀicial source: CFTC - Eight Things You Should Know Before Trading Forex
2.7 Why there is no single universal EUR/USD price
Because the spot FX market is decentralized, prices are formed across many venues and liquidity rela-
tionships. Major prices are normally close because arbitrage and competition connect markets, but tiny
differences can exist between liquidity providers or brokers. A chart on one retail platform is therefore a
representation of that broker/feed’s market data, not the output of one oﬀicial global exchange.
This is why you will later learn to distinguish:
• the market idea you are trading;
• the price feed used to analyze it;
• the execution venue/dealer through which you transact;
• the costs introduced by spread, commission, financing and slippage.
2.8 Example: a simple economic exposure
A Kenyan business expects to pay EUR 100,000 in three months. Today EUR/KES is hypothetical 150.
If the euro rises to 160 KES, the payment costs KES 1,000,000 more than it would at 150. The company
therefore has a genuine currency risk. A hedging transaction attempts to reduce uncertainty around that
future cost.
A retail speculator is different. The speculator deliberately accepts currency risk because they believe a
price movement may create a profit. That makes risk control essential: unlike the importer, the speculator
did not need the exposure in the first place.
2.9 Common beginner mistakes
• Thinking the retail broker is the forex market.
• Treating every FX product as identical.
• Assuming a huge market means profits are easy.
• Believing that being right about an economy guarantees being right about a currency trade.
• Ignoring the legal entity and product contract actually offered by a broker.
2.10 Exercises
1. In your own words, explain why EUR/USD is a relative price rather than an absolute price.
2. Give one example each of hedging, speculation and commercial currency exchange.
3. Create a two-column table comparing OTC retail forex/CFDs with exchange-traded FX futures.
4. Visit the BIS 2025 FX survey and record the shares of spot, forwards and FX swaps.

Commercial banks and dealers
Large banks intermediate customer flows, quote prices, manage inventories, hedge exposures and trade in
their own capacity within risk limits. Their role in price formation is much deeper than the retail stereotype
of a single "bank trader" placing directional bets.

Corporations
Corporations enter FX to pay suppliers, receive revenues, finance subsidiaries, hedge future cash flows and
manage balance-sheet exposures. Their motive may be risk reduction rather than profit from currency
direction.

Chapter 2 - Who Trades Forex and Why
Prices Move
3.1 Learning objectives
You should be able to describe the main participant groups in FX, distinguish liquidity demand from
directional speculation, and understand why a price can move even when the underlying economic news
seems unchanged.
3.2 The market is an auction of competing needs
At any moment, market participants have different motives. Some must transact. Some are hedging.
Some are taking directional views. Some are providing liquidity. Some are arbitraging price differences.
The exchange rate is the price at which enough willingness to buy and sell meets.
It is therefore misleading to imagine “buyers” fighting “sellers” as fixed teams. Every completed trans-
action has both a buyer and a seller. What changes the price is the aggressiveness and urgency of
order flow at available prices , together with changing expectations about future value.
3.3 Major participant groups
3.3.1 Commercial banks and dealers
Large banks intermediate customer flows, quote prices, manage inventories, hedge exposures and trade
in their own capacity within risk limits. Their role in price formation is much deeper than the retail
stereotype of a single “bank trader” placing directional bets.
3.3.2 Corporations
Corporations enter FX to pay suppliers, receive revenues, finance subsidiaries, hedge future cash flows and
manage balance-sheet exposures. Their motive may be risk reduction rather than profit from currency
direction.
36

Forex Trading From First Principles to Advanced Practice Version 1.0
3.3.3 Asset managers and pension funds
A global investment portfolio creates currency exposure whenever assets and liabilities are denominated
in different currencies. Funds may fully hedge, partially hedge or intentionally retain exposure.
3.3.4 Hedge funds and proprietary traders
These participants may trade macroeconomic views, relative value, momentum, carry, volatility, event
risk and many other strategies.
3.3.5 Central banks and sovereign institutions
Central banks manage reserves and may intervene in FX markets when consistent with their mandates
and policies. Monetary policy decisions also affect exchange rates indirectly through interest rates and
expectations.
3.3.6 Retail traders
Retail participants are small relative to the institutional market. Their advantage is not information
superiority or speed. Their potential advantages are flexibility, low organizational overhead, the ability to
stay flat, and the ability to choose only the strategies and time horizons they can execute well.
3.4 Price moves because expectations change
Suppose traders already expect a central bank to raise rates by 0.25 percentage points. The bank raises
by exactly 0.25. A beginner may ask, “Why didn’t the currency rise? Higher rates should strengthen it. ”
The answer is that expected information can already be reflected in price .
The more useful question is:
What happened relative to what the market had already priced?
Maybe the rate hike was expected, but the central bank signalled that no more hikes are likely. The new
information could actually be dovish relative to expectations, causing the currency to fall.
This concept - actual versus expected versus previously priced - becomes central in the macro
section.
3.5 Flow can matter even without new headlines
Prices can move because large portfolios rebalance, hedges are adjusted, liquidity is thin, stop orders
are triggered, or one-sided demand arrives. News is important, but not every price movement requires a
newspaper headline.
3.6 Liquidity and market depth
Liquidity is the ability to transact meaningful size with limited price impact. In a deep market, many
orders exist around the current price. In a thin market, the same aggressive order can move price farther.
Liquidity typically varies by:
37

Forex Trading From First Principles to Advanced Practice Version 1.0
• currency pair;
• time of day;
• market session overlap;
• holidays;
• scheduled economic releases;
• crisis conditions;
• dealer risk appetite.
You will later learn why spread and slippage can widen around high-impact events.
3.7 Example: the same news, different reaction
Imagine inflation is reported at 3.2%.
Scenario A: consensus expected 2.8%. Inflation is meaningfully hotter than expected, so traders may infer
tighter policy and higher yields.
Scenario B: consensus expected 3.6%. Inflation is lower than expected, so the same 3.2% number may be
interpreted as disinflationary.
The raw number is identical. The surprise is opposite.

Chapter 4
Chapter 3 - Currency Pairs, Quotes,
Pips and Cross Rates
4.1 Learning objectives
You should be able to read a currency quote correctly, identify base and quote currencies, calculate pip
changes, understand pip value conceptually, and derive simple cross rates.
4.2 Base and quote currency
In EUR/USD:
• EUR is the base currency .
• USD is the quote currency .
EUR/USD = 1.1700 means one unit of the base currency (1 EUR) costs 1.1700 units of the quote currency
(USD).
When you buy EUR/USD , you are economically long EUR and short USD. When you sell EUR/USD ,
you are short EUR and long USD.
That relationship should become automatic.
4.3 Major, minor and cross pairs
Common USD-major pairs include EUR/USD, GBP/USD, USD/JPY, USD/CHF, AUD/USD, NZD/USD
and USD/CAD. A cross pair does not contain USD, for example EUR/GBP or EUR/JPY.
Do not memorize labels as if they create trading value. What matters is understanding which economies,
policy regimes and exposures the pair represents.
4.4 What is a pip?
A pip is a conventional unit of price movement. For many pairs quoted to four decimal places, one pip is
0.0001. For many JPY pairs quoted to two decimal places in traditional convention, one pip is 0.01.
39

Forex Trading From First Principles to Advanced Practice Version 1.0
Example:
EUR/USD moves from 1.1700 to 1.1735.
Change = 0.0035 = 35 pips .
USD/JPY moves from 150.20 to 150.85.
Change = 0.65 = 65 pips .
Modern platforms often quote one extra decimal place. That fractional unit is sometimes called a pipette
or fractional pip.
4.5 Lots and notional value
Retail forex commonly uses lot terminology:
• 1 standard lot = 100,000 units of the base currency;
• 0.10 lot = 10,000 base units;
• 0.01 lot = 1,000 base units.
Broker contract specifications can differ, especially for CFDs outside major FX pairs, so always verify the
symbol’s contract size.
A position’s notional value is the economic amount controlled, not the cash margin deposited.
Example: buying 0.10 lot EUR/USD controls EUR 10,000 of base-currency notional.
4.6 Pip value - first principles
For a pair quoted in your account currency, pip value can be intuitive. If EUR/USD is traded in a
USD-denominated account:
For 1 standard lot (EUR 100,000), one pip = 100,000 x 0.0001 = USD 10 .
For 0.10 lot, approximately USD 1 per pip.
For 0.01 lot, approximately USD 0.10 per pip.
For pairs where the quote currency differs from the account currency, pip value must be converted. Your
platform can calculate it, but you need to understand the principle so you can detect impossible position
sizes.
4.7 Direct and indirect quotation
Whether a quote is called direct or indirect depends on the observer’s domestic currency. Do not over-
focus on the terminology. The operational rule is simpler: always identify which currency is base, which
is quote, and what one unit of base costs.
4.8 Cross-rate calculation
Suppose:
40

Forex Trading From First Principles to Advanced Practice Version 1.0
EUR/USD = 1.2000
GBP/USD = 1.5000
Then:
𝐸𝑈 𝑅/𝐺𝐵𝑃 ≈ 𝐸𝑈 𝑅/𝑈 𝑆𝐷
𝐺𝐵𝑃 /𝑈 𝑆𝐷 = 1.2000
1.5000 = 0.8000
This relationship helps explain why currency pairs are not independent. If two USD pairs move, the
corresponding cross rate must remain internally consistent enough to prevent obvious arbitrage.
4.9 Percentage return versus pip movement
A pip count alone does not tell you how meaningful a move is. A 100-pip move at EUR/USD 1.1000 is
about 0.91%, while a 100-pip move in a different pair or price level may represent a different percentage.
Professional risk thinking ultimately emphasizes volatility and percentage/risk units , not bragging
about pip totals.

Chapter 5
Chapter 4 - Bid, Ask, Spread and
Transaction Costs
5.1 Learning objectives
You should understand why every quote has a bid and ask, how spread creates an immediate transaction
cost, why advertised minimum spreads are not the same as realized cost, and how commission, financing
and slippage combine into all-in trading friction.
5.2 Two prices exist because liquidity has a cost
A typical retail quote may show:
EUR/USD bid: 1.1700
EUR/USD ask: 1.1702
The broker/liquidity stream is willing to buy from you at the bid and sell to you at the ask. If you buy
immediately, you generally transact near the ask. If you immediately close by selling, you transact near
the bid.
The difference is the spread:
𝑆𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑎𝑑 = 𝐴𝑠𝑘 − 𝐵𝑖𝑑
Here the spread is 0.0002 = 2 pips.
5.3 The immediate-loss intuition
Suppose you buy EUR/USD at 1.1702 while the bid is 1.1700. If nothing moves and you immediately
close, the round trip loses approximately the spread (plus commission, if any). This is why a strategy
with tiny gross profits can become unprofitable after realistic costs.
42

Forex Trading From First Principles to Advanced Practice Version 1.0
5.4 Fixed versus variable spreads
Some products advertise fixed-like conditions; many FX accounts use variable spreads that change with
market liquidity. Spreads can widen during:
• major data releases;
• central-bank announcements;
• market open/reopen periods;
• holidays;
• unexpected shocks;
• thin overnight conditions;
• sharp volatility.
A backtest that assumes the same tiny spread at all times can be dangerously optimistic.
5.5 Commission
Some account types quote tighter raw spreads and charge a separate commission per lot or per side.
Others embed more compensation in the spread. Compare all-in round-trip cost , not the headline
spread alone.
5.6 Slippage
Slippage is the difference between the price you expected/requested and the price actually filled. Slip-
page can be favourable or adverse, though retail traders often notice adverse slippage more. It becomes
especially important around gaps, news and fast markets.
5.7 Overnight financing / swap
Holding a leveraged FX/CFD position overnight can generate a financing debit or credit based on broker
methodology, interest-rate differentials, product design and markups. The amount can vary by day and
may include multi-day adjustments around settlement conventions or weekends.
Do not treat swap as an insignificant footnote. A strategy that holds positions for weeks can have
materially different net results after financing.
5.8 Currency conversion charges
If your account currency differs from the P/L or settlement currency, brokers may convert balances or
charges. That conversion can introduce additional cost.
5.9 The all-in cost model
A simplified model is:
𝑁 𝑒𝑡 𝑃 /𝐿 = 𝐺𝑟𝑜𝑠𝑠 𝑝𝑟𝑖𝑐𝑒 𝑃 /𝐿 − 𝑆𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑎𝑑 − 𝐶𝑜𝑚𝑚𝑖𝑠𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛 − 𝐹 𝑖𝑛𝑎𝑛𝑐𝑖𝑛𝑔 − 𝑆𝑙𝑖𝑝𝑝𝑎𝑔𝑒 − 𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑣𝑒𝑟𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛 𝑐𝑜𝑠𝑡𝑠
43

Forex Trading From First Principles to Advanced Practice Version 1.0
Not every component applies identically to every trade, but the principle is universal: gross chart profit
is not net account profit .
5.10 Example
A strategy earns an average gross +0.35R per winning/loss-weighted trade before costs. If average total
friction is 0.20R per trade, net expectancy is only +0.15R. If real costs rise to 0.40R during the hours you
actually trade, the system becomes negative.
That is why the reference roadmap requires cost stress testing rather than trusting idealized charts.
5.11 Broker-advertising trap
“Spreads from 0.0 pips” does not mean your average cost will be zero. The useful questions are:
• How often is that minimum available?
• During which sessions?
• Is commission charged?
• What is the average spread on your pairs and hours?
• How much slippage occurs in your actual order size?
• What are overnight financing terms?

Chapter 6
Chapter 5 - Orders and Execution
6.1 Learning objectives
You should understand market, limit and stop orders; stop-loss and take-profit instructions; order duration;
why a stop price is not always a guaranteed fill price; and how order choice interacts with liquidity.
6.2 Market order
A market order prioritizes execution over exact price. You are asking to transact at the best available
price under the broker/venue’s execution process. In fast markets, the actual fill can differ from the last
price you saw.
6.3 Limit order
A limit order specifies a price condition. A buy limit seeks to buy at the limit price or better; a sell limit
seeks to sell at the limit price or better. Limits prioritize price over certainty of execution. Price can
touch a level without your full order necessarily being filled under all market structures.
6.4 Stop order
A stop order becomes active when price reaches a specified trigger. Buy stops are commonly placed above
current market price; sell stops below. Stops can be used to enter breakouts or exit losing positions.
6.5 Stop-loss order
A stop loss is a risk-control instruction, not a magical guarantee that your loss can never exceed the
planned amount. In normal liquid conditions, execution may be close to the stop. In gaps or extremely
fast conditions, the next available fill may be worse.
This is one reason risk per trade must be conservative enough to tolerate occasional execution error.
45

Forex Trading From First Principles to Advanced Practice Version 1.0
6.6 Take-profit order
A take-profit order is a preplanned exit at a favourable price. Fixed targets are only one exit style. Other
systems may use trailing stops, opposite signals, time exits or volatility-based exits.
6.7 Stop-limit order
Some platforms/products support stop-limit orders, which trigger a limit rather than a marketable order.
They can reduce price uncertainty but introduce the risk of not being filled at all. Understand the exact
order types supported by your broker.
6.8 Time in force
Examples can include Good-Til-Cancelled (GTC), day orders and other broker-specific durations. Retail
FX platforms may implement durations differently. Read platform documentation rather than assuming
stock-market terminology transfers perfectly.
6.9 Entry quality versus strategy quality
Beginners often over-focus on finding the “perfect entry. ” A mediocre system cannot usually be rescued
by shaving one pip from every entry, while a robust strategy can tolerate some execution noise. Your job
is to specify an entry rule that is consistent, testable and appropriate for the market’s liquidity.
6.10 Example: breakout order
Suppose your rule is to enter long only after a completed H4 candle closes above the previous 55-bar high.
You have at least two conceptually different approaches:
1. Enter at the next bar’s market price after confirmation.
2. Place a stop order above the breakout level before the close.
These are not the same strategy because the information available and fill assumptions differ. Your
strategy specification must decide which one you are testing.
6.11 Execution journal
For serious demo/live trading, record:
• signal price;
• intended order type;
• requested price;
• actual fill;
• spread at entry;
• slippage;
• stop and target;
• any rejection or partial fill;
• whether the order followed the rulebook.

Chapter 6 - Margin, Leverage, Equity
and Stop-Out
7.1 Learning objectives
You should understand leverage mathematically, separate margin from risk, calculate basic account equity
and free margin, and explain how overleveraging can destroy an account even when a broker allows the
position.
7.2 Leverage is not the same as risk
This distinction is foundational.
Leverage describes how much notional exposure can be controlled relative to capital/margin.
Risk is how much you expect to lose if your stop or adverse scenario is reached.
A trader can use a high-leverage account but take small positions and therefore use very little effective
leverage. Conversely, a trader can use a low nominal leverage ratio but still risk far too much on a poorly
sized position.
7.3 Notional exposure
Suppose you buy EUR 100,000 worth of EUR/USD. Your notional exposure is EUR 100,000 even if the
broker only requires a fraction of that amount as margin.
7.4 Margin requirement
If a broker requires 1% margin on a position, controlling USD 100,000 equivalent would require approxi-
mately USD 1,000 of margin.
The reciprocal intuition is:
• 1% margin roughly corresponds to 100:1 maximum leverage on that position;
• 2% margin roughly 50:1;
48

Forex Trading From First Principles to Advanced Practice Version 1.0
• 5% margin roughly 20:1.
Exact broker calculations can differ by symbol and tier.
7.5 Balance, equity, used margin and free margin
• Balance: realized account value after closed transactions.
• Floating/unrealized P/L : profit or loss on open positions.
• Equity: balance plus floating P/L (and broker-specific adjustments).
• Used margin : capital reserved to support open leveraged positions.
• F ree margin: equity not currently committed as used margin.
• Margin level : commonly equity divided by used margin, expressed as a percentage, though platform
definitions should be verified.
A simplified relation:
𝐸𝑞𝑢𝑖𝑡𝑦 = 𝐵𝑎𝑙𝑎𝑛𝑐𝑒 + 𝑈 𝑛𝑟𝑒𝑎𝑙𝑖𝑧𝑒𝑑 𝑃 /𝐿
𝐹 𝑟𝑒𝑒 𝑀 𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑖𝑛 = 𝐸𝑞𝑢𝑖𝑡𝑦 − 𝑈 𝑠𝑒𝑑 𝑀 𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑖𝑛
7.6 Margin call versus stop-out
A margin call is a warning or condition indicating insuﬀicient margin under the broker’s rules. A stop-
out is the level at which the broker may automatically close positions to protect the account/broker from
further losses. Exact thresholds are contractual and vary.
Never design a risk plan that depends on reaching the broker’s stop-out. Your own stop and position
sizing should keep you far away from that point.
7.7 Example: available leverage does not justify position size
Account equity: USD 2,000.
Broker maximum: 1:400.
A naive trader may think, “I can control USD 800,000. ” That is the wrong question.
The correct questions are:
1. Where is the trade invalidated?
2. How far is the stop from entry?
3. How much of the account am I willing to risk?
4. What position size makes the cash loss at the stop equal to that risk budget?
If risk is 0.5%, the planned cash loss is only USD 10. The position may be tiny even though the broker
technically allows enormous leverage.

7.8 Kenyan regulatory context
Kenya’s online FX regulatory framework sets legal requirements for licensed providers and leverage pa-
rameters. A regulatory maximum is not a training recommendation. This course’s personal risk policy
is intentionally much stricter than any maximum leverage a broker may advertise.

8.5 Due-diligence checklist
Before live funding, verify:
1. Exact legal entity and CMA license number.
2. Account jurisdiction shown in your contract.
3. Client-money segregation policy.
4. Negative-balance and margin close-out policy.
5. Product type: FX, CFD, futures, or other derivative.
6. Spread and commission schedule.
7. Overnight financing methodology.
8. Order execution policy and slippage handling.
9. Complaint and dispute process.
10. Deposit/withdrawal ownership requirements.
11. Data export/history availability.
12. Platform/server identity.
13. Whether marketing claims match formal disclosures.

CFTC forex advisories identify recurring risks including unrealistic guaranteed returns, social-media solic-
itation, unregistered/offshore entities, pressure to deposit more, diﬀiculty withdrawing and schemes that
depend on recruiting or managed-account promises.
A useful rule:
If the sales pitch focuses on how easy the profits are rather than how the risk is controlled,
leave.
8.7 Binary-option style products
The original reference framework correctly separates regulated online forex/CFDs from binary-option-
style trading. Kenyan online FX rules restrict licensed online FX brokers from offering binary options.
Products that reduce trading to a short-horizon fixed payout “up/down” wager should not be treated as
equivalent to the curriculum in this book.
This is why platforms such as Expert Option are not part of the learning track presented here.

Chapter 10
Chapter 9 - OHLC, Candlesticks and
Timeframes
10.1 Learning objectives
You should be able to read OHLC data, explain what a candlestick represents without relying on pattern
names, distinguish chart timeframe from holding period, and understand why lower timeframes contain
more noise and execution friction.
10.2 A candle is compressed information
Every standard candlestick summarizes four prices for a fixed period:
• Open - the first traded/quoted price in the bar’s period;
• High - the highest price recorded during that period;
• Low - the lowest price;
• Close - the final price at the end of the period.
If close is above open, the candle is often displayed as bullish; if close is below open, bearish. Colours
differ by platform and have no analytical meaning beyond visual convenience.
The candle’s body shows the distance between open and close. The upper and lower wicks show excursions
beyond the body.
10.3 Read the story, not the nickname
Suppose an H1 candle opens at 1.1000, falls to 1.0960, rallies to 1.1040 and closes at 1.1030. A beginner
may try to assign a named candlestick pattern. A better first-principles reading is:
1. Sellers pushed price lower early in the hour.
2. That pressure failed to hold.
3. Buyers then pushed above the open.
4. The bar closed near its high.
58

Forex Trading From First Principles to Advanced Practice Version 1.0
That description is factual. Whether it has predictive value depends on context, market regime, location
and evidence.
10.4 Timeframes
A 5-minute candle compresses five minutes of market data. H1 compresses one hour. H4 compresses four
hours. D1 compresses a trading day according to the platform’s session/time convention.
The same market can look bullish on D1, sideways on H4 and bearish on M15. This is not contradictory.
Different timeframes describe different horizons.
10.5 Why beginners should start higher
This course initially prioritizes D1, H4 and H1 rather than scalping. Reasons include:
• more time to think before acting;
• transaction costs are usually smaller relative to the intended move;
• less temptation to overtrade;
• easier journaling;
• less sensitivity to millisecond execution;
• more visible macro and structural context.
This is a teaching choice, not a claim that lower timeframes can never be traded successfully.
10.6 Candle boundaries differ
Forex is a near-24-hour weekday market, so a daily bar depends on the data vendor/broker’s day boundary.
H4 bars may also start at different server times. That can slightly change indicator values and candle
shapes. When testing a strategy, use consistent data and record the source/time convention.
10.7 Non-standard charts
Renko, range bars, Heikin-Ashi and other transformed charts can be useful visualization tools, but they do
not represent raw time-based OHLC in the same way. Learn standard candles first. You must understand
exactly how a transformed chart is constructed before basing rules on it.

Chapter 10 - Swing Highs, Swing Lows
and Market Structure
11.1 Learning objectives
You should be able to identify significant swings, describe trend and range structure objectively, distinguish
a retracement from a confirmed structural reversal, and avoid forcing every chart into a trend label.
11.2 Market structure starts with turning points
A swing high is a local peak around which price stops rising and moves lower. A swing low is a local
trough around which price stops falling and moves higher.
Not every microscopic zigzag matters. Significance depends on timeframe and the trading process. On a
daily chart, a swing that develops over several days may be relevant; on M1, thousands of tiny fluctuations
may be irrelevant to a swing strategy.
11.3 Uptrend structure
A simplified uptrend is characterized by a sequence of:
• higher highs (HH);
• higher lows (HL).
A downtrend is characterized by:
• lower lows (LL);
• lower highs (LH).
A range lacks persistent directional progression and repeatedly trades between areas of demand/supply
or support/resistance.
61

Forex Trading From First Principles to Advanced Practice Version 1.0
11.4 Trend is descriptive, not predictive
Calling a market an uptrend means the recent price sequence has been upward. It does not guarantee
the next bar will rise. Trend labels organize information; they do not remove uncertainty.
11.5 Structural break versus noise
Suppose an uptrend has a major higher low at 1.1000. Price dips below a tiny intraday swing at 1.1080
but remains above 1.1000. It may be premature to declare a full reversal. Your strategy must define
which swing level matters.
This is why phrases such as “trend broke” are too vague for a rulebook. A testable version might say:
“D1 trend state becomes neutral when the close falls below the most recent confirmed 20-bar
swing low. ”
The specific rule can vary; the key is that it must be explicit.
11.6 Retracement versus reversal
A retracement is a temporary move against the prevailing trend that does not yet invalidate the trend
definition. A reversal is a change large enough to satisfy your defined condition for a new regime or
opposite trend.
You cannot reliably know in real time whether the first pullback candle is “just a retracement. ” You can
only apply predefined criteria and update as evidence arrives.
11.7 The fractal problem
Market structure is nested. A daily uptrend contains H1 downswings; an H1 downtrend may contain M5
rallies. This is why timeframe alignment later matters.

Chapter 11 - Support, Resistance and
Zones
12.1 Learning objectives
You should understand support/resistance as areas of prior market interaction rather than magical lines,
distinguish horizontal levels from trendlines, and develop an evidence-based way to annotate levels without
hindsight.
12.2 What support and resistance actually mean
Support is an area where downward movement previously met enough buying interest or reduced selling
pressure to slow/reverse price. Resistance is an area where upward movement previously encountered
enough selling interest or reduced buying pressure to slow/reverse.
They are descriptions of historical interaction, not promises that future orders are waiting at exactly the
same price.
12.3 Why zones are usually more honest than perfect lines
Markets trade continuously and spreads, data feeds and execution differ. A turn around 1.1000 may
involve 1.0992-1.1010 rather than one mathematically sacred point. Treat many levels as zones unless
your strategy has a specific price rule.
12.4 Sources of commonly watched areas
• major prior swing highs/lows;
• range boundaries;
• previous day/week highs/lows;
• prior breakout levels;
• round numbers;
• gaps in products where true gaps occur;
• trendline/channel boundaries;
64

Forex Trading From First Principles to Advanced Practice Version 1.0
• high-volume areas in markets where centralized/reliable volume data are available.
12.5 Role reversal
An old resistance area can become support after a breakout, and vice versa. But this is not a law. The
useful question is whether a systematic rule exploiting such behaviour survives testing.
12.6 Touch count trap
Beginners often believe more touches automatically make a level stronger. Repeated tests can also consume
resting liquidity or indicate pressure building toward a break. Do not accept folklore without evidence.
12.7 Drawing discipline
When annotating levels in replay:
1. use only information visible at the current replay bar;
2. mark broad major levels first;
3. avoid adding ten lines until one appears to work;
4. record why each level existed before the future unfolded;
5. remove levels that no longer matter according to your rule.
This prevents hindsight art.
12.8 Trendlines
A trendline connects selected lows in an uptrend or highs in a downtrend. Because the choice of anchor
points can be subjective, use trendlines primarily as descriptive tools until you can specify an objective
rule for testing them.

13.1 Learning objectives
You should understand what a breakout is, why false breakouts are inevitable, how volatility and closing
criteria affect breakout definitions, and why entry timing must be specified in advance.
13.2 Breakout definition
A breakout occurs when price moves beyond a defined boundary such as a range high, swing high, Donchian
channel or other objective level.
The word “breakout” is incomplete without a rule. Does price merely trade one tick above the level?
Must a candle close above it? How far? On which timeframe? Does volume matter? Is there a retest
requirement?
Each definition produces different trades.
13.3 Why false breakouts happen
A false breakout occurs when price moves beyond a boundary but fails to continue and returns inside.
This can happen because:
• the initial flow was insuﬀicient;
• liquidity above/below the level absorbed the move;
• stops were triggered but new directional demand did not follow;
• the market remained range-bound;
• a news impulse reversed;
• the breakout was real on one timeframe but trivial on another.
False breakouts are not evidence that “the market hunted your stop. ” Stop clusters can affect flow, but
attributing every loss to manipulation is an excuse that prevents learning.
66

13.4 Consolidation and volatility compression
Markets often alternate between quieter ranges and directional expansions. Compression can precede
expansion, but direction is not known simply because volatility is low. A breakout strategy needs both a
trigger and a risk/exit framework.
13.5 Closing confirmation
Requiring a completed candle close beyond a level reduces some intrabar false breaks but enters later and
can increase stop distance. There is no free confirmation. Every filter trades one problem for another.
13.6 Retest entry
Waiting for price to return to the breakout area may improve entry price in some cases but can miss moves
that never retest. Again, it is a separate strategy variant and must be tested separately.
13.7 Donchian example
A simple research hypothesis from the reference framework is:
• long when an H4 close exceeds the highest high of the previous 55 completed bars;
• short when it closes below the lowest low;
• use a volatility-based stop;
• exit on an opposite channel or trailing rule.
The exact numbers are not sacred. The value of the example is that it is objective enough to test without
hindsight.

14.4 A verage True Range (ATR)
ATR averages True Range over a chosen lookback. ATR does not predict direction. It is a volatility
estimator.
If EUR/USD D1 ATR is 50 pips, a 100-pip stop is 2 ATR. If ATR later rises to 100 pips, the same 100-pip
stop is only 1 ATR and may be much tighter relative to normal movement.
14.5 Fixed pips versus volatility units
A fixed 20-pip stop may be enormous during a quiet M15 session and tiny during a major H4 macro move.
Volatility-based stops attempt to scale the invalidation distance with current market behaviour.
This does not mean “always use 2 ATR. ” It means volatility should be considered explicitly and any
multiple should be tested.
14.6 Risk connection
If you risk a fixed 0.5% of equity and the stop doubles from 50 to 100 pips, your position size should
roughly halve, all else equal. That is a key survival principle:
V olatility rises -> stop distance often rises -> position size falls -> cash risk stays
controlled.
14.7 Volatility regimes
Markets can shift between low- and high-volatility regimes. A strategy that worked during calm conditions
may behave differently in crisis periods. Later you will evaluate strategies by regime rather than assuming
stationarity.

15.5 Crossover systems
The familiar 50/200 SMA crossover is not recommended because the numbers are magical. It is useful as
a transparent benchmark:
• long when shorter average crosses above longer;
• short when it crosses below;
• enter according to a predefined next-bar rule;
• define stop/risk/exit;
• test across pairs and periods.
The reference framework warns against testing dozens of nearby combinations until one looks spectacular.
A result based on 47/193 may simply be accidental if you searched hundreds of alternatives.
15.6 Momentum
Momentum means recent price movement tends to persist for some horizon. Academic research has
documented time-series momentum across diversified futures/forward markets, including currencies, over
historical samples. This provides a plausible research foundation for trend strategies, not a guarantee that
one specific retail rule will remain profitable.
Research reference: Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen - Time Series Momentum
15.7 Indicator redundancy
Five indicators derived from the same closing-price series do not create five independent pieces of evidence.
For example SMA, EMA, MACD and some oscillators share underlying price information. Learn what
each transformation measures rather than counting confirmations.

Chapter 15 - Oscillators: RSI, MACD,
Bollinger Bands and Misuse
16.1 Learning objectives
You should understand what common indicators mathematically represent, when they are descriptive
rather than predictive, and why “overbought” does not automatically mean “sell. ”
16.2 RSI
The Relative Strength Index (RSI) compares average recent gains with average recent losses and transforms
the result to a 0-100 scale. Common thresholds such as 70 and 30 are conventions, not physical laws.
A strong trend can remain “overbought” for a long period. Therefore:
RSI > 70 does not logically imply the next move must be down.
A strategy using RSI needs an exact rule and evidence under defined regimes.
16.3 MACD
MACD is based on the difference between exponential moving averages, often combined with a signal line.
It is essentially a transformation of trend/momentum information already in price.
16.4 Bollinger Bands
Bollinger Bands typically place bands around a moving average at a multiple of recent standard deviation.
They describe the relationship between current price and recent variability.
Touching an upper band does not mean price is “too high” in any universal sense. In strong trends, price
can repeatedly move along an outer band.

Forex Trading From First Principles to Advanced Practice Version 1.0
16.5 Stochastic oscillator
Stochastic measures where the close sits relative to a recent high-low range. Like RSI, extreme values can
persist in strong trends.
16.6 Divergence
Divergence compares price highs/lows with an indicator’s highs/lows. It can be visually compelling and
highly subjective. If you use divergence later, define pivot selection, lookback and confirmation objectively
before testing.
16.7 The regime problem
Mean-reversion oscillators may appear useful in ranges and repeatedly fail in trends. Trend filters may
help, but every filter changes the strategy and must be validated rather than added because it “looks
better. ”
16.8 Indicator rule
For every indicator you use, answer:
1. What raw data does it transform?
2. What mathematical quantity does it represent?
3. What parameter(s) are chosen?
4. What trading hypothesis does it support?
5. What evidence shows the rule works after costs?
If you cannot answer all five, the indicator is decoration.

17.1 Learning objectives
You should recognize common formations, understand the behavioural stories often associated with them,
and separate descriptive pattern literacy from statistical evidence.
17.2 Why learn patterns at all?
Patterns provide a shared visual vocabulary. Terms such as double top, triangle, flag, head-and-shoulders
and engulfing candle help traders describe repeated shapes eﬀiciently.
The danger is jumping from:
“This shape exists”
to:
“This shape has a reliable edge. ”
Those are different claims.
17.3 Common price patterns
17.3.1 Double top / double bottom
Two attempts around a similar extreme with an intervening retracement. A strategy must define tolerance,
minimum separation and what counts as confirmation.
17.3.2 Head and shoulders
A three-peak structure with the middle peak higher, often interpreted as weakening trend structure.
Subjective neckline placement can create hindsight.

17.3.3 Triangles and wedges
Price range contracts between converging boundaries. Breakout direction is not guaranteed by the shape
alone.
17.3.4 Flags and pennants
Short consolidations following a directional impulse. The useful question is whether a precisely defined
continuation rule survives testing after costs.
17.4 Candlestick patterns
Doji, hammer, shooting star, engulfing and similar names can be useful shorthand. But a single candle
ignores:
• prior trend;
• nearby structure;
• volatility regime;
• scheduled news;
• broader timeframe;
• transaction costs.
A hammer in the middle of random noise is not the same setup as the same candle after a multi-week
decline at a defined support area.
17.5 Evidence discipline
Use Murphy and other technical texts to learn the vocabulary. Use Aronson’s evidence-based approach
later to decide which objective rules deserve belief.
The reference roadmap intentionally states that technical-analysis books should be read as language and
hypothesis sources , not proof that every pattern has a permanent edge.

18.1 Learning objectives

18.2 A practical three-layer model
For early swing-trading education, use:
1. Context timeframe - D1.
2. Setup timeframe - H4.
3. Execution/refinement timeframe - H1.
This is not the only valid stack. The benefit is consistency.
18.3 Context, setup, trigger
Suppose D1 is in a broad uptrend. H4 is pulling back toward a prior breakout zone. H1 produces a
breakout from a small consolidation.
These are three different pieces of information:
• D1 describes broader context;
• H4 identifies the area/setup;
• H1 provides the precise trigger.
If your strategy uses them, each role must be documented in advance.
18.4 The timeframe-shopping trap
A trader loses on H1 and then says, “But D1 was bearish,” or wins and says, “H4 confirmed it. ” If you
select whichever timeframe supports your conclusion after the fact, analysis becomes unfalsifiable.

19.1 Learning objectives
You should understand the core macro variables that drive central-bank policy and currency expectations:
output, inflation, employment, interest rates, money/credit conditions and productivity.
19.2 Why macro matters in FX
Currencies are monetary assets. Their relative value is influenced by expectations about growth, inflation,
interest rates, policy credibility, capital flows and risk. Technical analysis describes what price has done;
macro analysis helps explain why relative demand for currencies can change .
You do not need a degree in economics. You do need a clean mental model.
19.3 Gross domestic product (GDP)
GDP measures the value of final goods and services produced within an economy over a period. Real
GDP adjusts for price changes; nominal GDP does not.
A common expenditure identity is:
𝐺𝐷𝑃 = 𝐶 + 𝐼 + 𝐺 + (𝑋 − 𝑀 )
where:
• 𝐶 = consumption;
• 𝐼 = investment;
• 𝐺 = government spending;
• 𝑋 − 𝑀 = net exports.
83

Forex Trading From First Principles to Advanced Practice Version 1.0
Faster growth can support a currency if it leads markets to expect tighter monetary policy or stronger
capital inflows. But growth is not mechanically bullish: if growth is already fully expected, the currency
may not react.
19.4 Inflation
Inflation is the rate at which the general price level rises. Distinguish:
• inflation: prices rising;
• disinflation: inflation rate falling while prices may still rise;
• deflation: general price level falling.
Central banks care about the persistence, composition and expectations surrounding inflation, not only
one monthly print.
19.5 Employment and wages
Labour-market data help policymakers assess demand pressure, slack and wage-driven inflation risks.
Important concepts include:
• payroll/job growth;
• unemployment rate;
• labour-force participation;
• job vacancies;
• wage growth;
• hours worked;
• productivity.
Strong employment can be currency-supportive if it raises expected interest rates, but again the surprise
versus expectation matters more than a simple good/bad label.
19.6 Interest rates
Interest is the price of borrowing money and the reward for lending/saving. Central-bank policy rates
influence short-term market rates and broader financial conditions.
FX markets are especially sensitive to relative expected rate paths . A 4% rate in Country A is not
automatically bullish versus Country B if markets expect A to cut rapidly while B stays at 3.5%.
19.7 Real interest rates
A simplified real-rate approximation is:
𝑅𝑒𝑎𝑙 𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑒 ≈ 𝑁 𝑜𝑚𝑖𝑛𝑎𝑙 𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑒 − 𝐸𝑥𝑝𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑒𝑑 𝑖𝑛𝑓𝑙𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛
If nominal rates are 5% and expected inflation is 3%, the approximate real rate is 2%. Markets often care
about real yields because they influence the real return available on currency-denominated assets.

19.8 Productivity
Productivity measures output produced per unit of input such as labour. Strong productivity can sup-
port sustainable wage growth and economic growth without identical inflation pressure. It can therefore
influence long-run rates, profits and currency valuation.
19.9 Supply versus demand shocks
A demand-driven boom may push both growth and inflation higher, encouraging tighter policy. A negative
supply shock can reduce growth while raising inflation, creating a harder central-bank trade-off. The same
inflation number can therefore have different implications depending on its cause.

Chapter 19 - How Central Banks Move
Markets
20.1 Learning objectives
You should understand central-bank mandates, policy rates, monetary-policy transmission, reaction func-
tions, forward guidance, quantitative easing/tightening and why the market trades the expected future
path, not only today’s decision.
20.2 What a central bank is trying to do
Mandates differ by jurisdiction, but major central banks generally pursue some combination of price
stability, employment/output stability and financial-system stability.
Examples:
• The U.S. Federal Reserve operates under a mandate commonly summarized as maximum employment
and price stability.
• The ECB targets price stability with a symmetric 2% medium-term inflation objective.
• The Bank of England operates monetary policy to meet the U.K. government’s inflation target.
• The Bank of Japan defines a 2% price-stability target.
Always use the central bank’s own current policy framework rather than a trading blog’s summary.
20.3 Policy transmission
A simplified transmission chain is:
Simplified transmission chain: Policy decision -> money-market rates -> borrowing/saving costs ->
financial conditions -> demand/employment -> inflation.
Exchange rates are part of those financial conditions. A tighter expected policy path can raise domestic
yields and attract capital, but the relationship depends on relative conditions and risk.
86

Forex Trading From First Principles to Advanced Practice Version 1.0
20.4 Reaction function
A reaction function is your mental model of how policymakers are likely to respond to the economy. It
asks:
• What variables matter most now?
• How persistent does the central bank think inflation is?
• How much labour-market weakness will it tolerate?
• Is policy restrictive or accommodative?
• What risks could change the path?
The reaction function is more useful than memorizing “CPI up = hike. ”
20.5 Forward guidance
Central banks communicate expected policy direction through statements, projections, minutes, speeches
and press conferences. Guidance is conditional, not a promise. Markets constantly compare new language
with prior communication.
20.6 Quantitative easing (QE)
When conventional rates are constrained or broader easing is desired, central banks may purchase assets
to lower longer-term yields, improve market functioning or loosen financial conditions. QE can affect
currencies through yields, risk appetite and relative policy stance.
20.7 Quantitative tightening (QT)
QT describes balance-sheet normalization or runoff that reduces central-bank asset holdings/liquidity
support. Its market effects depend on pace, implementation and expectations.
20.8 Decision versus path
A central bank can:
• hike today but sound dovish about the future;
• hold today but signal future hikes;
• cut today but imply cuts will be slower than markets expected.
The currency usually reacts to the change in expected path , not the isolated action.

Federal Reserve
21.1 Learning objectives
You should understand why the U.S. dollar occupies a central role in global FX, how the Fed’s mandate
and Treasury market affect dollar pricing, and which U.S. data deserve regular attention.
21.2 The dollar’s special role
The U.S. dollar is the most heavily traded currency in global FX. BIS 2025 data show it on one side of
roughly 89% of FX transactions. Many commodities, trade invoices, international debts and reserve assets
are also dollar-linked.
That means USD moves are influenced not only by the U.S. domestic economy but also by global demand
for dollar funding, risk aversion and international portfolio flows.
21.3 The Fed’s dual mandate
The Federal Reserve seeks maximum employment and stable prices. Traders monitor:
• FOMC rate decisions;
• statement language;
• Chair press conference;
• Summary of Economic Projections when released;
• meeting minutes;
• speeches from influential oﬀicials;
• balance-sheet policy.

21.4 Core U.S. data
21.4.1 CPI
Published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). CPI measures consumer-price changes. Markets care
about headline, core, monthly and annual rates, details and revisions/seasonal effects.
Oﬀicial schedule: BLS Release Calendar
21.4.2 Employment Situation / Nonfarm Payrolls
The monthly employment report includes payroll employment, unemployment, earnings and other labour-
market measures. Revisions can be important.
Oﬀicial source: BLS Employment Situation
21.4.3 PCE inflation
The Personal Consumption Expenditures price index is published by the Bureau of Economic Analysis
and is an important measure in Fed analysis.
Oﬀicial source: BEA PCE Price Index
21.4.4 GDP
BEA publishes advance, second and third estimates as data are updated.
Oﬀicial schedule: BEA Release Schedule
21.4.5 Other data
Also monitor, when relevant: retail sales, ISM surveys, job openings, initial claims, housing, industrial
production, trade and consumer expectations.
21.5 Treasury yields and USD
U.S. Treasury yields reflect expected policy, inflation, growth, term premium and supply/demand. Rising
yields can support USD, especially if the move represents a relative increase versus foreign yields, but
relationships vary by regime.
21.6 Safe-haven and funding dynamics
During stress, USD can strengthen even if U.S. data are weak because global investors seek liquid dollar
assets or need dollar funding. This is why macro relationships are conditional rather than permanent
formulas.

22.1 Learning objectives

How to Read Them Properly
26.1 Learning objectives
You should be able to interpret a data release using previous, consensus, actual and revision; distinguish
levels from rates of change; and avoid trading headlines without understanding methodology.
26.2 The four numbers you need
For a scheduled release, record:
1. Previous - prior published value.
2. Consensus - surveyed/market expectation before release.
3. Actual - newly released value.
4. Revision - change to a previously published estimate.
A good surprise calculation is conceptually:
𝑆𝑢𝑟𝑝𝑟𝑖𝑠𝑒 = 𝐴𝑐𝑡𝑢𝑎𝑙 − 𝐸𝑥𝑝𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑒𝑑
But the sign must be interpreted economically. A lower unemployment rate may be a “positive” surprise,
while lower inflation can be dovish in another context.
26.3 Level versus change
GDP can be discussed as annualized quarterly growth, quarter-on-quarter growth or year-on-year growth.
Inflation can be monthly or annual. Payrolls are changes in employment levels. PMI is an index. Mixing
definitions creates mistakes.
Always record the unit.
100

26.4 Revisions
Economic data are estimates. Revisions can materially change the story. If payrolls beat expectations but
prior months are revised sharply lower, the market may interpret the report as weaker than the headline.
26.5 Seasonal adjustment
Many data series are seasonally adjusted to remove predictable seasonal patterns. Trading based on raw
numbers without understanding adjustments can be misleading.
26.6 Base effects
Year-on-year inflation can change because the comparison month one year earlier was unusually high or
low. Base effects can make annual inflation fall even when current monthly inflation remains firm.
26.7 High-impact releases to master
• CPI/HICP/PCE inflation;
• employment/payrolls/unemployment/wages;
• GDP;
• PMIs/ISM surveys;
• retail sales/consumption;
• central-bank decisions;
• trade/current account;
• industrial production;
• inflation expectations.
26.8 Oﬀicial-source habit
Economic calendars are convenient, but when a release matters, read the oﬀicial statistical release .
Aggregator headlines can omit methodology, revisions and composition.
Useful oﬀicial calendars:
• U.S. BLS
• U.S. BEA
• Eurostat
• U.K. ONS

30.1 Learning objectives
You should understand current account, capital/financial flows, trade balance, foreign investment and

30.2 Balance-of-payments intuition
A country’s external transactions are recorded across current-account and financial/capital flows. A
simplified current account includes trade in goods/services plus income and transfers.
A current-account deficit means the country is, in aggregate, spending/investing more abroad than it
receives from certain external income flows and must be financed by capital inflows or reserve changes
under accounting identities.
30.3 Trade balance
Exports create potential foreign demand for the domestic currency; imports create demand for foreign
currencies. But modern FX markets are dominated by financial flows as well as trade, so a trade surplus
does not guarantee appreciation.
30.4 Portfolio flows
Foreign investors buying domestic bonds/equities may need the local currency or hedge the FX exposure.
The hedge ratio matters. A stock-market inflow does not automatically create an unhedged currency
inflow.
30.5 Foreign direct investment (FDI)
Long-term investment in productive assets can create persistent capital flows but occurs on a different
horizon from daily speculative trading.

30.6 Reserve management
Central banks hold foreign reserves and may change reserve composition or intervene, affecting FX flows.

Chapter 34 - Probability: The Language
of Trading
35.1 Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you should be able to separate outcome from decision quality, calculate basic
trading expectancy, explain why a profitable method can lose repeatedly, and describe why no single trade
can prove or disprove an edge.
35.2 First principle: a trade is one observation from a distribution
A trading decision is made before the outcome is known. A well-designed trade can lose and a reckless
trade can win. If you judge process only by the most recent P/L, you train yourself to repeat lucky
mistakes and abandon good rules after ordinary losses.
Think of a strategy as generating a distribution of R-multiples rather than a sequence of predictions.
The important questions become:
• how often does it win?
• how large is the average winner?
• how large is the average loser?
• how variable are outcomes?
• what do costs remove?
• how deep are ordinary losing streaks and drawdowns?
35.3 Expectancy
If outcomes are measured in units of initial risk, a simple expectancy formula is:
𝐸(𝑅) = 𝑃 (𝑊 ) × 𝑊𝑅 − 𝑃 (𝐿) × 𝐿𝑅
where 𝑃 (𝑊 ) is win probability, 𝑊𝑅 is average winner in R, 𝑃 (𝐿) is loss probability and 𝐿𝑅 is average
loss in R.
121

Forex Trading From First Principles to Advanced Practice Version 1.0
35.3.1 Example 1: low win rate, positive expectancy
A system wins 40% of trades. A verage winner = +2R. A verage loser = -1R.
𝐸 = 0.40(2) − 0.60(1) = +0.20𝑅
The strategy loses more often than it wins but has positive expectancy before any omitted costs.
35.3.2 Example 2: high win rate, negative expectancy
A system wins 80% of trades. A verage winner = +0.25R. A verage loser = -1.50R.
𝐸 = 0.80(0.25) − 0.20(1.50) = −0.10𝑅
An 80% win rate can still lose money.
35.4 Sample expectancy is not the true expectancy
If you observe +0.2R average over 25 trades, that does not prove the true long-run expectancy is +0.2R.
Small samples are noisy. A few unusually large winners can dominate. This is why the reference framework
prefers roughly 200-300 aggregated observations where feasible and requires out-of-sample evidence rather
than trusting a tiny sample.
35.5 Variance and sequencing
Suppose a strategy has 45% winners. A sequence such as L-L-W-L-L-L-W-W-L is not evidence that the
strategy has stopped working. With randomness, wins and losses cluster.
The psychological skill is not to expect alternating wins and losses. The research skill is to compare actual
drawdown and rolling expectancy with the distribution seen in historical and forward testing.
35.6 Outcome quality matrix
Decision Outcome Correct interpretation
Rule-compliant Win Good process, favourable outcome
Rule-compliant Loss Good process, unfavourable outcome
Rule-breaking Win Bad process, favourable luck
Rule-breaking Loss Bad process, unfavourable outcome
The most dangerous cell is rule-breaking + win because it rewards bad behaviour.

37.1 Learning objectives

37.2 The order of decisions
A professional risk sequence is:

2. determine the logical invalidation/stop location;
3. measure stop distance;
4. choose permitted risk percentage;
5. calculate cash risk;
6. calculate position size.
Do not choose a large lot size first and squeeze the stop to make the cash loss fit.
37.3 Cash risk
Cash Risk = Account Equity × Risk Fraction
Example: USD 2,000 equity at 0.5% risk:
2, 000 × 0.005 = $10
37.4 Pip value when quote currency equals account currency
For most non-JPY pairs, one pip is 0.0001. If you trade 100,000 EUR/USD units:
127

100, 000 × 0.0001 = 10USD per pip
For 10,000 units, pip value is USD 1. For 1,000 units, about USD 0.10.
37.5 Position size formula
When pip value per unit in account currency is known:
Units = Cash Risk
Stop Pips × Pip Value per Unit
37.5.1 Example: EUR/USD
Equity = USD 2,000. Risk = 0.5% = USD 10. Stop = 50 pips.
Required pip value:
10/50 = $0.20per pip
Since 1,000 EUR/USD units are approximately USD 0.10/pip, the position is approximately 2,000 units
= 0.02 standard lot.
37.6 JPY pairs
For many JPY pairs a pip is 0.01. A 100,000-unit USD/JPY position has a pip value of:
100, 000 × 0.01 = 1, 000JPY per pip
If the account is in USD, convert that JPY pip value back into USD using the current USD/JPY rate. At
USD/JPY = 150.00, the approximation is:
1, 000/150 ≈ $6.67per pip
Because exchange rates change, pip value can change.
37.7 Cross-currency pairs
If your account currency is neither base nor quote currency, calculate pip value in the pair’s quote currency
and then convert it to your account currency using the relevant exchange rate. Your platform’s calculator
can help, but you must understand the conversion logic before relying on it.
37.8 KES-funded or KES-denominated accounts
A KES account does not imply you are trading a KES currency pair. Kenya’s regulations restrict licensed
online FX brokers from offering currency pairs involving the Kenyan shilling, while an account/funding

If a broker only allows a minimum position size that forces you to risk more than your policy, skip the

38.5 Risk of ruin
“Risk of ruin” broadly asks: what is the probability that the trading process reaches a loss threshold from
which the trader cannot or will not continue? Exact formulas depend on assumptions about fixed versus
fractional betting, independence and outcome distribution. Do not rely on a single simplistic formula for
a real strategy.
The practical controls are:
• positive expectancy after costs;
• small fractional risk;
• no martingale;
• maximum open risk;
• drawdown pause rules;
• enough capital and position-size granularity;
• willingness to retire a broken strategy.
38.6 Maximum drawdown is not a permanent constant
A historical maximum drawdown is only the worst drawdown observed in that sample . The future
can be worse. A sensible live plan therefore requires headroom beyond the backtest maximum and an
investigation trigger before the account approaches intolerable loss.
38.7 The reference framework’s review thresholds
Training policy:
• review a weak week around -4R or worse;

Chapter 38 - Stops, Targets and Exit
Logic
39.1 Learning objectives
You should understand the different purposes of protective stops and exit rules, distinguish structural from
arbitrary stops, and evaluate exits as part of a complete strategy rather than after-the-fact storytelling.
39.2 A stop is an invalidation and risk-control mechanism
A protective stop answers: At what market condition is the trade idea suﬀiciently wrong that
I will exit? The cash risk is then controlled by position size.
Bad logic:
“I only want to lose USD 10, so I will put the stop 5 pips away. ”
Better logic:
“The setup is invalid 42 pips away. At my permitted cash risk, what size can I trade?”
39.3 Common stop frameworks
39.3.1 Structure stop
Placed beyond a swing/level whose break invalidates the setup.
39.3.2 Volatility stop
Uses an objective volatility measure such as ATR to avoid placing stops inside ordinary noise.
39.3.3 Time stop
Exits if the expected move does not develop within a defined period.
133

Forex Trading From First Principles to Advanced Practice Version 1.0
39.3.4 Emergency/catastrophic stop
Protects against a scenario the normal exit logic may not handle.
39.4 Targets and exits
Possible exit families include:
• fixed reward multiple;
• opposing structure level;
• trailing stop;
• moving-average/trend reversal;
• channel exit;
• time exit;
• event-driven exit;
• scaling/partial exit, if explicitly researched.
None is universally best. Exit logic changes win rate, average win, trade duration and costs.
39.5 Trailing stops
A trailing stop can allow large trends to develop but may surrender open profit. If you test a 2 x ATR
trail and a 3 x ATR trail, treat them as distinct hypotheses rather than choosing whichever looks best
after seeing the whole chart.
39.6 Stop widening
The course prohibits widening a stop because a losing trade “needs more room. ” If a wider stop is genuinely
superior, it must be specified and retested as a new strategy version. A rule changed mid-trade is not
research; it is discretion under pressure.
39.7 Gaps and slippage
A stop order is not a guarantee of the exact stop price. During illiquidity, major news or weekend gaps,
execution may occur worse than the stop trigger. Position sizing should therefore leave headroom for tail
events.

40.2 One pair contains two exposures
Long EUR/USD = long EUR + short USD.

trade.
A gross expectancy of +0.12R becomes only +0.02R net. A small change in spread or slippage could
remove the edge entirely.
41.4 Frequency amplifies friction
A strategy trading twice per month can tolerate a different cost structure from one trading 20 times per
day. High turnover repeatedly pays the spread/commission and is more sensitive to latency and slippage.
This is one reason the course begins with higher timeframes rather than encouraging beginner scalping.

41.5 Swap/financing
Holding leveraged positions overnight can generate debits or credits based on broker terms, currency-rate
differentials and product pricing. The amount can vary by pair, day and broker. Some days may have
multi-day rollover adjustments due to settlement conventions. Use the actual contract specification rather
than assumptions.
41.6 Cost stress test
The reference framework requires a robustness test around 1.5x normal assumed transaction costs .
A strategy that collapses under a modest increase is fragile.
41.7 Break-even spread exercise
Suppose a strategy’s gross expectancy is +0.15R and all other costs are 0.05R. It can tolerate at most
roughly another 0.10R average friction before expected net return reaches zero. This is not a prediction;
it is a sensitivity calculation.

Chapter 42 - Capital, Compounding and

43.1 Learning objectives
You should understand why skill and account size are separate constraints, why return targets should
come after evidence, and why trading capital must be financially expendable without being psychologically
disposable.
43.2 A profitable edge can still produce small cash returns
Suppose two traders have identical net performance of 8% over a year:
• Trader A: USD 1,000 capital -> USD 80 before tax/withdrawal effects.
• Trader B: USD 50,000 capital -> USD 4,000.
The strategy did not become “better” in the larger account. Capital converted the same percentage result
into a larger cash amount.
This creates a dangerous temptation: a small-account trader may use excessive leverage to force salary-
sized returns. That changes the risk distribution and often destroys the account.
43.3 Do not reverse-engineer risk from an income target
Bad process:
“I need KES X this month, so I must make Y% and increase lot size. ”
Better process:
“My tested system has this observed distribution. I will risk the permitted fraction and accept
that returns are variable. ”
142

Forex Trading From First Principles to Advanced Practice Version 1.0
43.4 Compounding
If capital grows and you maintain fixed fractional risk, position size gradually grows. If capital falls, size
automatically shrinks. This is mathematically different from increasing risk percentage after wins.
43.5 Withdrawals
Withdrawals reduce the capital base and therefore future position sizes under fixed fractional risk. A
professional plan separates:
• trading capital;
• emergency savings;
• living expenses;
• tax reserve;
• withdrawals.
Never use rent, debt repayments, emergency funds or borrowed money as trading capital.
43.6 When can trading be considered income?
Not after a profitable week, month or even a short demo run. Before relying on trading for living costs,
require a long live record across different conditions, adequate capital, tax planning, a cash buffer outside
the trading account and evidence that withdrawals do not force excessive risk.
This course intentionally does not prescribe a target annual return. Your own validated live distribution
must come first.

Chapter 44 - Trend Following From First
Principles
45.1 Learning objectives
You should understand what a trend-following strategy is trying to capture, why it often has many small
losses and occasional larger wins, and how to turn trend concepts into objective rules.
45.2 The hypothesis
Trend following does not require predicting the beginning or end of every trend. The hypothesis is that
price movement may persist long enough, often enough, for a rule that cuts losses and stays with sustained
moves to have positive expectancy after costs.
Academic evidence for time-series momentum across diversified futures/forwards, including currencies,
makes trend/momentum a defensible research starting point. It does not prove that any specific moving
average or retail implementation will remain profitable forever.
Research reference: Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen - Time Series Momentum
45.3 Moving-average baseline
The supplied roadmap proposes a transparent learning baseline:
• instruments initially: EUR/USD, GBP/USD, USD/JPY, AUD/USD;
• timeframe: Daily;
• long: 50-day SMA crosses above 200-day SMA, enter only after the completed signal bar according to
specified execution logic;
• short: opposite crossover;
• initial stop: 2 x ATR(14);
• exit: opposite crossover or a separately tested trailing-stop variant;
• demo/backtest risk: 0.5%;
• initial live risk: 0.25%;
• total open risk cap: 1.5%.

This is a benchmark to learn testing , not a recommendation to trade it with real money.
45.4 Trend filters versus entries
A long-term moving average can be used as:
• an entry trigger;
• a directional filter;
• an exit;
• a regime classifier.
These are different strategy designs. Do not switch roles after seeing results.
45.5 Whipsaw
Trend systems often lose repeatedly in sideways markets. This is not automatically a defect; it is a
structural cost of waiting for sustained moves. The relevant question is whether larger trends compensate
over a broad sample after costs.

Chapter 48 - Carry With a Trend Filter
49.1 Learning objectives
You should understand carry as compensation linked to rate differentials and financing, why it can reverse
violently, and why actual broker swap terms must be included.
49.2 Carry is not free interest
Currencies differ in interest rates. Holding one currency against another can create a financing advantage
or disadvantage, but the exchange rate itself can move by far more than the accumulated financing.
Research on currency carry finds systematic risk rather than a free arbitrage. High-carry portfolios can
suffer sharp reversals.
Research reference: Lustig, Roussanov & Verdelhan - Common Risk Factors in Currency Markets
49.3 Educational carry + trend hypothesis
The reference framework suggests:
• liquid G10/major pairs;
• only consider a direction when the broker’s actual overnight financing is favourable after charges;
• require a trailing 3-month return to agree with carry direction;
• Daily timeframe;
• weekly review;
• initial 2 x ATR(20) stop as a testable starting choice;
• lower 0.25% risk because carry reversals can be abrupt;
• include actual financing debits/credits in testing.
Again: a research exercise, not a live signal.
49.4 Forward points and retail swap are not identical concepts
Institutional forward pricing is tied to spot and interest-rate differentials under no-arbitrage relationships,
while a retail broker’s overnight financing schedule includes the broker’s product construction and charges.

51.1 Learning objectives

51.2 Rules-based does not mean automated

51.3 Discretion does not mean random
A discretionary process may evaluate context that is diﬀicult to reduce to one formula. But it still needs
repeatable criteria. For example:

• defined macro scenarios;
• defined entry trigger;
• fixed risk;
• documented invalidation.

Ambiguous rules allow the trader to rewrite history:

the trend was not clean. ”
This creates hindsight bias and makes testing meaningless.

53.1 Learning objectives
You should be able to test a strategy with future information hidden, create a complete trade log and
resist skipping valid losers.
53.2 Backtest question
A useful backtest asks:
“Would these exact rules plausibly have produced an edge using information available at the
time?”
It does not ask:
