53.3 Manual replay protocol
1. Select historical start date without choosing it for a known trend.
2. Hide future bars using Bar Replay or equivalent.
3. Advance only enough to make each decision.
4. Record every valid signal.
5. Enter according to the frozen execution rule.
6. Record spread/cost assumption.
7. Record stop/exit exactly.
8. Take screenshots where helpful.
9. Never skip a loser because it “looked bad. ”
10. Never add a winner that violated the rule.

61.1 Learning objectives
You should recognize the most common decision biases in your own journal and design countermeasures.
61.2 Outcome bias
Judging a decision by whether it won. Countermeasure: grade rules before looking at P/L.

Losses can feel more painful than equivalent gains feel pleasurable. It can cause premature winners and

61.7 Anchoring
Fixating on entry price, a prior high, analyst forecast or target as if it were intrinsically important.
61.8 Overconfidence
Often increases after a winning streak. It can appear as larger size, more trades or rule exceptions.

61.9 A vailability bias

61.10 Hindsight bias
After the fact, the move appears obvious. Replay with future bars hidden is a direct antidote.
61.11 Gambler’s fallacy
Believing that after several losses a win is “due. ” Unless outcomes have a validated dependence structure,
a losing streak does not create entitlement to the next win.

Chapter 76 - Advanced Market

77.1 Learning objectives
You should understand that the institutional FX market is fragmented, distinguish dealer/interdealer/customer
flow at a high level and avoid pretending that a retail chart shows the entire order book.
77.2 A fragmented OTC market
The global FX market is not one centralized spot exchange. Trading occurs through bilateral dealer
relationships, electronic communication networks, single-dealer platforms, multi-dealer venues and other
arrangements. Different participants see different liquidity.
The Bank for International Settlements’ Triennial Survey is the best starting point for understanding the
scale and instrument mix of the market: https://www.bis.org/statistics/rpfx25_fx.htm
77.3 Dealer role
A dealer may:
• quote bid/ask prices;
• internalize opposing customer flow;
• hedge residual exposure elsewhere;
• manage inventory and credit limits;
• source liquidity from other dealers/venues.
A retail platform abstracts almost all of this complexity.
77.4 Liquidity is conditional
A pair can be highly liquid on average and temporarily illiquid around:
• market open/close transitions;
221

• major releases;
• holidays;
• unexpected shocks;
• very large flows.
Liquidity has dimensions: spread, depth, resilience and market impact. A narrow displayed spread is not
the whole concept.
77.5 Last look and execution conventions
Institutional electronic FX can involve execution practices and venue-specific rules unfamiliar to retail
traders. You do not need operational mastery, but you should recognize that dealer pricing/execution
involves more than the chart.
77.6 FX Global Code
The FX Global Code is a set of global principles of good practice for the wholesale FX market. It is not
a retail trading strategy and not a substitute for local law. Read its overview to understand professional
expectations around ethics, governance, execution, information sharing, risk management and settlement.

78.2 Why forward rates differ from spot
If two currencies have different interest rates, a no-arbitrage relationship links spot, forward and those

𝐹 = 𝑆 × 1 + 𝑟𝑞𝑢𝑜𝑡𝑒𝑇

where 𝑆 is spot, 𝐹 is forward and 𝑇 is time in years under simplified conventions.
The exact market formula uses currency-specific day-count conventions and compounding. The point is
conceptual: the forward rate is not simply a dealer’s prediction of where spot will be.
78.3 Covered interest parity intuition
If investors could borrow cheaply in one currency, convert at spot, invest at a higher rate in another and
lock the future conversion at a forward rate for a guaranteed profit, arbitrage would pressure prices until
the relationship is aligned, subject to funding/credit/basis effects.
78.4 Forward premium/discount
A currency can trade at a forward premium or discount relative to spot because of interest-rate differentials.
Do not interpret the forward price mechanically as a forecast.

An FX swap combines:

Chapter 83 - Volatility Regimes,
Clustering and Range Expectations
84.1 Learning objectives
You should understand volatility clustering, why average ATR is not constant and how strategy/risk
behaviour can differ across regimes.
84.2 Volatility clusters
Large moves often occur near other large moves and quiet periods near quiet periods. This persistence is
called volatility clustering. It does not mean every high-volatility day predicts another large move, but
volatility is not independent white noise.
84.3 ATR as local scale
ATR adapts to recent range. A 50-pip stop may be very wide in a quiet regime and very tight in a crisis.
Expressing distances relative to ATR helps compare scale, though ATR itself is backward-looking.
84.4 Volatility and position sizing
If stop distance expands with volatility while cash risk is fixed, position size falls. This is a natural risk
stabilizer.
84.5 Regime transitions
The most diﬀicult periods often occur when volatility changes rapidly. A strategy optimized for stable
quiet conditions may experience slippage and failed assumptions when volatility explodes.

deviations in cross-currency funding relationships.

transacts at bid.

tity/model.
Bullish - expecting or describing upward price tendency.

ing/exchange exposure.

transactions; terminology depends on statistical framework.

alongside FX price risk.

execution.

within its mandate.

tional material.
Commission - explicit broker/exchange fee charged for a transaction.
Consensus - market/economist expectation before an economic release.

with FX forward premium/discount.
Correlation - statistical measure of co-movement; unstable and not proof of causation.
COT (Commitments of T raders) - CFTC reports on reportable futures/options positioning categories.
Counterparty risk - risk that the other party to a financial contract fails to meet obligations.
CPI - consumer price index, a common inflation measure.
Cross pair - currency pair not involving USD, such as EUR/GBP.
Cross rate - exchange rate derived/quoted between two currencies, often via relationships to another
currency.

under relevant statistics.

real-money settlement.
Depth of market (DOM) - displayed liquidity/order information for a specific venue/provider, not a
universal FX order book.

antee it.

payoff distribution.

in research.

amount.

GDP - gross domestic product, a measure of economic output.

NFP - U.S. nonfarm payrolls component of the Employment Situation report.

Parameter - chosen numerical setting in a rule, such as moving-average lookback.

PCE price index - U.S. price measure produced by BEA, important to Fed analysis.

pairs and 0.01 for many JPY pairs.

118.6 Update policy
This course is dated 19 August 2026 . Before using any changing fact in live trading:
1. re-open the linked primary source;
2. verify the publication/update date;
3. verify the exact broker/entity/product/jurisdiction;
4. save a dated copy/screenshot where appropriate for your records;
5. do not let a changed regulation, central-bank framework or broker term silently invalidate your old
notes.
118.6.1 Review frequency
• Broker licensing/entity: immediately before opening/funding and periodically thereafter.
• Broker costs/product terms: before every strategy validation and periodically in live trading.
• Central-bank mandate/framework: when studying that currency and after major policy-review an-
nouncements.
• Tax law/KRA guidance: before first filing/meaningful withdrawals and each tax year.
• Platform documentation: whenever a feature/behaviour materially affects execution/testing.
118.7 Closing principle
A textbook can teach you what to understand and how to test it . It cannot make uncertainty
disappear. Your objective is not to become certain about the next EUR/USD candle. It is to become
competent enough to recognize uncertainty, define a process, risk little, collect evidence and refuse to
trade when the evidence or discipline is not good enough.
That is the standard this course is designed to enforce.
